parts.title: Breaking down medicine factory sludge with hot water and oxygen, with and without added helpers
parts.abstract:
Abstract

We tested a way to clean up the sludge left over from making medicines. We call this method wet oxidation: we heat the sludge in water under high pressure and add oxygen, so that the harmful material in it breaks down. We also tried adding catalysts, which are substances that speed up a reaction without being used up. Some of these catalysts dissolve in the water (homogeneous catalysts), and one is a solid that stays separate from the water (a heterogeneous catalyst).

Our results show that wet oxidation is a promising way to break down medicine sludge very efficiently. We judged how well it worked in two ways. The first is the share of the sludge's organic material that was removed, which we call VSS (volatile suspended solids). The second is the share of the sludge's chemical oxygen demand (COD) that was removed. COD measures how much oxygen it would take to break down the material in the sludge, so it tells us how much pollution is left.

Under the best conditions, we removed 86.8% of the VSS and 62.5% of the COD. These conditions were 260 °C for 60 minutes, with oxygen added at a starting pressure of 1.0 MPa (about ten times normal air pressure).

Adding sodium hydroxide (NaOH, a strong alkali) sped up the removal of VSS very well. With 10 grams of NaOH per litre, we removed 95.2% of the VSS under the same conditions of 260 °C for 60 minutes and a starting oxygen pressure of 1.0 MPa.

We also made a solid catalyst from copper and cerium on a support of aluminium oxide (written Cu–Ce/γ-Al2O3). With 10 grams of this catalyst per litre, we removed 87.3% of the VSS and 72.6% of the COD, again at 260 °C for 60 minutes with a starting oxygen pressure of 1.0 MPa.

The reaction gives off heat, and this heat can keep the reaction going by itself. The process produces small carboxylic acids, such as acetic acid. These could be sold and used as a food for the bacteria that clean wastewater in treatment plants. The leftover inorganic material can be used to make building materials. Together, these results suggest that catalytic wet oxidation is a promising way to shrink the amount of medicine sludge and to turn it into something useful.

Subject terms: Pollution remediation, Pollution remediation
parts.introduction_first:
Factories that make medicines produce large amounts of sludge. This sludge is a serious risk to the environment, because it contains harmful organic pollutants that are hard to break down. Medicine sludge is a complicated and dangerous kind of industrial waste, because it holds many different poisonous substances. In particular, it contains fairly high levels of organic material that dissolves in water, heavy metals, and antibiotics that are hard to break down, such as benzylpenicillin, aureomycin and berberine hydrochloride. For these reasons, it should be treated as hazardous waste.

More and more people are interested in finding good ways to treat medicine sludge. In the past, two methods have been used. One uses living things, such as bacteria, to digest the sludge. The other is burning it. Both have problems. The poisonous substances kill the bacteria, so the biological method works poorly. Burning only moves the pollution from the liquid into a solid or into the air, and it releases harmful gases such as sulphur oxides, nitrogen oxides and furans. On top of this, getting rid of the sludge is complicated and expensive. So there is a strong need for a treatment that works well, costs little and is kind to the environment.
parts.conclusion:
Conclusions

In this work, we studied wet oxidation of medicine sludge, both on its own and with several different catalysts added. Our results show that wet oxidation is a promising way to break down medicine sludge very efficiently.

Under the best conditions, we removed 86.8% of the VSS and 62.5% of the COD. These conditions were 260 °C for 60 minutes, a starting oxygen pressure of 1.0 MPa, and a starting COD of 15,000 mg·L−1.

Dissolving metal ions can greatly improve how well wet oxidation works. These include nickel (Ni2+), iron (Fe3+), copper (Cu2+) and cerium (Ce3+). Sodium hydroxide (NaOH) can also speed up the breakdown of the sludge, especially the removal of VSS. With 10 grams of NaOH per litre, we removed 95.2% of the VSS at 260 °C for 60 minutes, with a starting oxygen pressure of 1.0 MPa. However, adding NaOH held back the removal of COD.

We made the Cu–Ce/γ-Al2O3 catalyst by a standard method called wet impregnation, in which the support is soaked in a solution of the metals. With this catalyst, we removed 87.3% of the VSS and 72.6% of the COD at 260 °C over 60 minutes, with a starting oxygen pressure of 1.0 MPa and 10 grams of catalyst per litre.

Here is how the reaction works. First, the heat breaks the sludge apart in the water, a step called thermal hydrolysis. This produces a mixture of dissolved organic compounds and solid inorganic material. Next, the dissolved organic compounds react with free radicals, which are very reactive fragments of oxygen molecules that form in the hot, high-pressure water. This produces carboxylic acids such as acetic acid. These small carboxylic acids could be sold and used as a food for the bacteria that clean wastewater. The leftovers, which are mostly inorganic solids, can be fed into the furnace where cement is made, or added to building materials.

As for energy, the reaction gives off heat as the pollutants are broken down, and this heat can keep the reaction going. For these reasons, wet oxidation can be seen as an ideal way to shrink the amount of medicine sludge and to turn it into something useful.
parts.introduction_rest:
Wet oxidation is one of many methods that researchers have studied for shrinking and treating sludge. In this process, the organic pollutants are turned into small carboxylic acids, carbon dioxide, water and inorganic salts, and no harmful gases are released. The small carboxylic acids formed along the way can be used to help anaerobic fermentation, a process in which bacteria break down material without oxygen. This makes wet oxidation an interesting choice for breaking down activated sludge, the sludge that contains the bacteria used to clean wastewater.

Gasso and colleagues reported that a compact reactor with a jet mixer, which stirs the sludge with a high-speed stream of liquid, is a promising way to carry out wet oxidation. However, to remove and convert a reasonably large share of the sludge, wet oxidation needs high temperatures and high pressures.

Over the past few decades, many studies have looked at catalytic wet air oxidation, which is wet oxidation with a catalyst added, and most of this work has focused on developing better catalysts. Adding a catalyst can lower the temperature needed, make the reaction faster, and shorten the time the sludge must stay in the reactor.

Among the many catalysts tried, those containing copper (Cu2+) or cerium (Ce3+) have drawn a lot of attention, because they work well for breaking down wastewater and sludge. Wang and colleagues studied wet air oxidation of wastewater from medicine factories using a copper-based system. They showed that it can greatly improve how easily bacteria can break down organic wastewater that is poisonous, harmful and hard to break down. Copper ions can also act as efficient catalysts. Zhang and colleagues reported that a catalyst made from copper and nickel together, using microwaves and built with a flat, two-dimensional structure, worked even better.

Sodium hydroxide (NaOH) has also been reported to work as a catalyst that dissolves in the water when alcohols are broken down. Several studies of catalytic wet oxidation of organic compounds have also shown that NaOH speeds up the reaction. The hydroxide part of NaOH (OH−) is thought to start or help the reaction by pulling a hydrogen particle, called a proton, off the oxygen–hydrogen group of the molecules. NaOH affects not only how fast the reaction goes, but also which products it makes.

However, only a few studies have used real sludge from industry. That is why it is important to test how well wet oxidation treats real medicine factory sludge.

In this study, we tested wet oxidation of medicine sludge, both on its own and with several different catalysts added. We measured how much of the VSS and of the COD was removed.
parts.methods:
## Materials and methods

### What the medicine sludge was like

We collected the medicine sludge from a factory in eastern China that makes medicines from chemicals bought in, rather than from natural raw materials. We took the sludge from the part of the factory where it is thickened, and kept it at 4 °C until we needed it.

Before any treatment, the sludge had a COD of 15,000–16,000 mg/L. It held 13.5–13.8 g of VSS in every litre, and VSS made up 39–40% of all the solid material in the sludge. Its pH was 7.5–8.0, which means it was slightly alkaline, the opposite of acidic. We used the sludge just as it arrived, without treating it in any way first.

We bought our chemicals from Shanghai Sinopharm Chemical Reagent Co., Ltd. These were copper nitrate (Cu(NO3)2), cerium nitrate (Ce(NO3)3), nickel nitrate (Ni(NO3)2), iron sulphate (Fe2(SO4)3) and sodium hydroxide (NaOH). All of them were of analytical grade, which means they were very pure, and we used them just as they came, without cleaning them further. The oxygen we used to break down the sludge was ordinary industrial gas bought from a supplier.

### How we set up the experiments

We ran every experiment in a 100 mL stainless steel (SUS316) autoclave reactor, shown in Fig. 1. An autoclave is a sealed metal container that can be heated and pressurised, a bit like a pressure cooker. Ours was stirred by a motor. We bought it from Anhui Kemi Machinery Technology Co. Ltd, China24.

An electric heating jacket wrapped around the reactor let us set the temperature anywhere from 180 to 260 °C. We also changed the starting oxygen pressure from 0.2 to 1.0 MPa. The reactor was stirred at 300 turns per minute.

A typical experiment went like this. We put 50 mL of the sludge solution into the reactor, along with a certain amount of catalyst if we needed one, and then closed the reactor. We added the oxygen at the start. First we flushed the reactor several times to push out the nitrogen gas inside, and then we filled it with oxygen to the pressure we wanted.

Next, we heated the reactor to the temperature we had chosen. As the water heated up, it turned into steam, and the steam's own pressure built up inside the sealed reactor. We counted the moment the reactor reached the chosen temperature as the start of the reaction, which we call zero time. When the reaction had run for the time we wanted, we took the reactor out of the oven and let it cool to room temperature. Once the liquid had cooled, we took samples and analysed them.

Figure 1

Diagram of the reactor we used for wet oxidation.

### How we measured things

To measure VSS, we first dried the samples at 105 °C for 2 hours. We then burned them at 550 ± 50 °C for 4 hours, a method called the ignition loss method. The weight that burns away is the VSS. We weighed the samples after they had cooled in a desiccator, a sealed container that keeps things dry.

We measured COD with the potassium dichromate method, using a Hach Heating System (Hach Corporation, USA). In this method, a chemical called potassium dichromate breaks down the organic material, and we measure how much of it gets used up. We measured pH with a pH meter (pH-201, Hanna Corporation, Italy).

To see the surface shapes and textures of the catalysts we made, and of the support they were built on, we used a scanning electron microscope (Agilent 8500 FE-SEM). This microscope uses a beam of electrons instead of light, so it can show very fine detail. To find out which chemical elements the catalysts contained, we used X-ray diffraction (XRD-7000, Japan), a Siemens model that uses a type of X-ray called Cu-Kα radiation.
parts.results:
## Results and discussion

### Wet oxidation of medicine sludge

We looked at several conditions that might change how much pollution is removed. These were the reaction temperature, the reaction time, the starting oxygen pressure and the starting COD. Under the best conditions, we removed 86.8% of the VSS. These conditions were 260 °C for 60 minutes, a starting oxygen pressure of 1.0 MPa and a starting COD of 15,000 mg·L−1. At the same time, we removed as much as 62.5% of the COD.

Temperature made a big difference (Fig. 2a). The higher the temperature, the more VSS and COD we removed. Raising the temperature from 240 to 260 °C did not help VSS removal much. This is most likely because thermal hydrolysis, the step where heat breaks the sludge apart in water, was already nearly finished at 240 °C. COD removal, however, was still not high. This may be because wet oxidation mainly turns the organic material into small carboxylic acids, such as formic acid or acetic acid. These are not easily broken down further in hot, high-pressure water, so the COD was not fully broken down.

We conclude that higher temperatures help wet oxidation of medicine sludge. In practice, though, higher temperatures cost more to run.

Time also mattered (Fig. 2b). The longer we ran the reaction, the more VSS and COD we removed. Because thermal hydrolysis happens easily in a short time, VSS removal was much higher than COD removal for the same reaction time.

Oxygen played an important part in removing both VSS and COD. As Fig. 2c shows, COD removal went up as the oxygen pressure went up. We expected this, because adding more of the substance that does the breaking down (here, oxygen) usually makes the reaction faster. These results show that high oxygen pressure effectively removes organic compounds that are hard to break down and that are poisonous.

A high starting COD means the sludge liquid holds a lot of pollution. So the higher the starting COD, the smaller the share of VSS and COD we removed (Fig. 2d). In other words, wet oxidation became less efficient at removing the total amount of pollution. If the starting COD was too low, the reaction could not give off enough heat to keep itself going. Taken together, these results suggest that wet oxidation is a promising way to break down medicine sludge very efficiently.

Figure 2

How the reaction conditions affect the share of VSS and COD removed.

### How dissolved metal salts affect removal

We tested four dissolved metal salts as catalysts: copper nitrate (Cu(NO3)2), cerium nitrate (Ce(NO3)3), nickel nitrate (Ni(NO3)2) and iron sulphate (Fe2(SO4)3). We ran each one at 200, 220, 240 and 260 °C, for 60 minutes, with a starting oxygen pressure of 1.0 MPa and 0.2 grams of catalyst per litre.

Temperature again played an important part (Fig. 3a). In particular, raising the temperature from 200 to 220 °C increased COD removal by more than 25%. Compared with running the reaction without any catalyst, the dissolved catalysts raised COD removal by up to more than 10%. This shows that the catalysts we chose can speed up wet oxidation of medicine sludge. Of the four, copper (Cu2+) helped the most. With copper at 260 °C, we removed about 70% of the COD, the highest value we found.

VSS removal improved only a little compared with COD removal (Fig. 3b). It usually rose by about 3–5%. Copper and cerium (Ce3+) had a clear effect. As the temperature rose from 200 to 260 °C, VSS removal went from about 70% to about 90%. Even at 200 °C, we removed about 70% of the VSS. This means thermal hydrolysis happens easily, compared with what we saw for COD. The highest VSS removal was almost 90%, while the highest COD removal was only 70%. This may be because thermal hydrolysis dissolved the sludge into the water. Wet oxidation of the pollutants in that liquid may then produce acetic acid and other small carboxylic acids, which are not easily broken down further.

Figure 3

How dissolved metal ions affect the share of COD (a) and VSS (b) removed.

### How sodium hydroxide (NaOH) affects removal

Several earlier studies have shown that NaOH can act as a dissolved catalyst in wet oxidation of organic compounds. The hydroxide part of NaOH (OH−) is thought to start or help the reaction by pulling a hydrogen particle (a proton) off the hydroxyl group of a molecule. NaOH changes not only how fast the reaction goes, but also which products the reaction makes [22]. So we ran experiments to find out how NaOH affects the process. We changed the amount of NaOH added, the reaction temperature and time, and the starting oxygen supply (Fig. 4a–d).

Fig. 4a shows that VSS removal rose sharply as we added more NaOH. The most VSS we removed, 95.2%, came with 10.0 grams of NaOH per litre. In that same case, we removed 57.3% of the COD. Interestingly, adding NaOH lowered COD removal. This may be because NaOH made acetic acid build up, and acetic acid is a compound that is hard to break down [25].

The carboxylic acids made during wet oxidation are easy to deal with in biological wastewater treatment. So the liquid left after wet oxidation could be used to raise the BOD/COD ratio of wastewater. BOD is the oxygen that bacteria use up while digesting the material in the water. A higher BOD/COD ratio means the wastewater is easier for bacteria to digest.

Compared with the metal ions in Fig. 3, NaOH helped VSS removal more, even though the metal ions were better catalysts for removing COD. These results showed that adding NaOH greatly increased the breakdown of the sludge.

Figure 4

How NaOH affects the share of VSS and COD removed.

### Making the Cu–Ce/γ-Al2O3 catalyst

Among the many catalysts used in catalytic wet oxidation, those containing copper (Cu2+) or cerium (Ce4+) have drawn a lot of attention, because they work well for breaking down wastewater and sludge. Copper-based catalysts work less well when the water is very acidic or very alkaline. They have also been studied a great deal over the last ten years, because the chemical reactions that copper takes part in are more stable [26,27]. In our own earlier work, we tested several catalysts for wet oxidation of medicine sludge and wastewater. We found that the Cu–Ce/γ-Al2O3 catalyst we made worked well [28–30].

We made the catalyst by wet impregnation, a standard method. First, we mixed copper nitrate and cerium nitrate in equal amounts (a 1:1 molar ratio) in a solution of 1.0 mol/L. Then we soaked the aluminium oxide support (γ-Al2O3) in this solution for 24 hours. After soaking, we washed the solid three times with deionized water (very pure water with the dissolved salts removed). We dried it at 120 °C overnight and then heated it strongly at 550 °C for 4 hours.

Fig. 5 shows what the finished catalyst is like. We used X-ray diffraction (XRD), which shines X-rays at a solid to reveal the crystals inside it. Fig. 5a,b shows the results before and after we added the metals. Before adding the metals, the pattern showed only the peaks of the aluminium oxide. After adding the metals, new peaks from the copper oxide and cerium oxide (CuO–CeO2) clearly appeared. We then used this catalyst for catalytic wet oxidation of medicine sludge.

Figure 5

What the finished catalyst is like, as shown by X-ray diffraction.

### How the Cu–Ce/γ-Al2O3 catalyst affects removal

We tested how well our catalyst worked for catalytic wet oxidation of medicine sludge [30]. The highest removal was 87.3% of the VSS and 72.6% of the COD. We reached these values at 260 °C over 60 minutes, with a starting oxygen pressure of 1.0 MPa and 10 grams of catalyst per litre.

As Fig. 6a shows, COD removal went up as we added more catalyst. VSS removal, however, hardly changed when we added the catalyst. This suggests that COD and VSS may be removed by different chemical routes.

Temperature also had a strong effect (Fig. 6b). Raising the temperature from 180 to 240 °C greatly increased the removal of both COD and VSS, but going from 240 to 260 °C brought no clear improvement. This is most likely because the COD was not fully broken down, even though the organic pollutants in the sludge were almost completely broken down. In addition, the acetic acid made during wet oxidation is not easily broken down further in hot, high-pressure water.

Fig. 6c shows the effect of reaction time. The share removed rose gradually as time went on. At first, though, COD removal did not increase. After 20–30 minutes, it rose sharply. The reason may be that, as the reaction went on, organic material moved from the solid sludge into the liquid, so COD removal improved a lot. As the small in-between products in the liquid were used up, COD removal slowed down.

Fig. 6d shows the effect of the starting oxygen pressure. It strongly affected the removal of both COD and VSS. COD removal rose sharply as the pressure went from 0.2 to 0.6 MPa. These results mean that high oxygen pressure can speed up the reaction and remove organic compounds effectively, leading to high removal of both COD and VSS [31].

Figure 6

How the Cu–Ce/γ-Al2O3 catalyst affects the share of VSS and COD removed.

### How we think the reaction works

Wet oxidation is usually thought of as a reaction driven by free radicals. So far, very few studies have looked at how wet oxidation of sludge actually works, so the reaction steps for some organic compounds are still unclear. Wet oxidation always makes large amounts of in-between products, so its reaction steps are always very complicated.

For wet oxidation of medicine sludge, we propose the steps shown in Fig. 7. In the first step, thermal hydrolysis breaks the sludge apart. This gives a mixture of dissolved organic compounds and solid inorganic material. As a result, VSS removal was very high even with a very short reaction time and fairly low temperatures.

In the second step, the dissolved organic compounds react with free radicals that form from oxygen gas in the hot, high-pressure water. This produces carboxylic acids such as acetic acid. These small carboxylic acids, including acetic acid, may be useful for further commercial development. They can be used as a source of carbon for the bacteria that clean wastewater.

With more than 90% of the VSS removed, the leftovers of the sludge, which are mostly inorganic solids, can easily be used to make building materials. As for energy, the reaction gives off heat as the pollutants are broken down, and this heat can keep the reaction going by itself. For these reasons, catalytic wet oxidation can be seen as an ideal way to treat medicine sludge.

Figure 7

The steps we propose for wet oxidation of medicine sludge.
